lessons.title: Major keys with four sharps or flats

objectives: Name a major key with four sharps or four flats
E major has four sharps; A♭ major has four flats
Every major key up to four accidentals is now within reach

concept.title: The fourth accidental
concept.body: Grade 2 took the sharp keys as far as A major's three and the flat keys as far as E♭ major's three. One more of each completes the set for this grade. E major has four sharps, adding D♯ after F♯ C♯ G♯. A♭ major has four flats, adding D♭ after B♭ E♭ A♭. Nothing new is happening — the order never varies and no accidental is ever skipped — so the count alone still names the key. Read the signature left to right, count what you see, and stop: four sharps is E major, four flats is A♭ major.

teach.smartTip: Four sharps is E major; four flats is A♭ major.
teach.didYouKnow: The last sharp in a signature is always the seventh note of the key, a semitone below the keynote — so E major's final D♯ sits just under E. Spotting that last sharp names the key without counting.

objectives: The six new relative pairs: B minor with D major, G minor with B♭ major, F♯ minor with A major, C minor with E♭ major, C♯ minor with E major, F minor with A♭ major
Two new major keys arrive alongside these pairs: E major (4 sharps) and A♭ major (4 flats)
How to count a minor 3rd down from a major tonic to find its relative minor

concept.title: Grade 3 minor keys
concept.body: Six more minor keys join the syllabus, each sharing a key signature with a major key. B minor pairs with D major, G minor with B♭ major, F♯ minor with A major, C minor with E♭ major, C♯ minor with E major, and F minor with A♭ major. E major and A♭ major are new this grade too — E major has four sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯), and A♭ major has four flats (B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭). As before, the relative minor's tonic sits a minor 3rd below its major partner's.

teach.smartTip: Count three semitones — a minor 3rd — down from the major tonic and you'll land on the relative minor, two letter-names lower: D down to B, B♭ down to G, A down to F♯, E♭ down to C, E down to C♯, A♭ down to F.
teach.didYouKnow: C♯ minor and F♯ minor are this course's first minor keys with a sharp in their own name — their key signatures still work exactly the same way as any other minor key.

lessons.title: Degrees up to four sharps and flats

objectives: Name any note of a major scale by its degree number
The keynote is the 1st degree, so the count starts at one, not zero
The rule is the same in every key up to four accidentals

concept.title: Counting from the keynote
concept.body: Nothing new happens to the rule. The keynote is the 1st degree, and the numbers count letter names up from it in whatever key the signature names. With four sharps and flats now in scope the keynote may be E, A♭, F♯ or C♯, and the degrees follow it exactly as they followed C at Grade 1. Grade 3 also asks for intervals above the tonic by number **and** type, and those two ideas fit together: the interval from the 1st degree to the 5th is a 5th, so the degree number and the interval number are the same count.

teach.smartTip: The degree number and the interval above the keynote are the same count. Find the keynote and count letters.
teach.didYouKnow: Degrees are the reason a chord chart written in Roman numerals transposes for free. The numbers are positions, so they survive a key change untouched.

lessons.title: Tonic triads up to four accidentals

objectives: Build the tonic triad of a major key in root position
The tonic triad is the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees stacked
Root position means the keynote is the lowest note

concept.title: Three notes that fix the key
concept.body: The tonic triad is the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees, and that holds in E major and A♭ major exactly as it held in C. The signature supplies the accidentals: E major's triad is E, G♯ and B, and every one of those sharps is already in the signature, so nothing is written on the note. Build from the letters, check the signature, and only add an accidental if the key does not already give it to you.

teach.smartTip: Letters first, signature second. E-G-B in E major reads as E, G♯, B without writing a single accidental.
teach.didYouKnow: This is why a key signature is worth having at all. Without one, E major's tonic triad would need a sharp written on the G every time it appeared.

objectives: Recognise the Grade 3 words for energy and attitude
A character word says how the music should sound, not how fast it goes
Con brio and con forza pair 'with' to a noun

concept.title: How it should feel, not how fast
concept.body: Most of what Grade 3 adds is not about speed at all. This half is about drive. *Agitato* is agitated, *animato* animated, *energico* energetic. Some are attitudes rather than energies: *deciso* with determination, *risoluto* bold, *maestoso* majestic. Two come as a noun you meet with 'con': *con brio* is with vigour, *con forza* with force — the word after 'con' is a thing, not a description, which is why it needs the 'con' at all. A tempo marking says how fast; these say what it should sound like at that speed.

teach.smartTip: These do not change the speed. Allegro con brio is the same tempo as allegro, played with more bite.
teach.didYouKnow: Beethoven marked a movement 'con brio' more often than almost any other composer. It is the difference between the right notes and the right performance, and the only part a metronome cannot help with.

objectives: Recognise the Grade 3 words for weight, touch and mood
These describe how the music should feel, not how fast it goes
Semplice asks for the opposite of all of them — play it plainly

concept.title: How heavy, and how it feels
concept.body: This half of the Grade 3 vocabulary is about weight and mood. *Leggiero* is light and nimble, *pesante* heavy, *delicato* delicate, *sostenuto* sustained. The moods run from *tranquillo* calm to *triste* sad to *scherzando* joking. And *semplice* asks for none of it — play the passage plainly, without adding character of your own. None of these changes the tempo. A piece marked andante tranquillo goes at exactly the speed andante asks for; the second word tells you what it should sound like when it gets there.

teach.smartTip: None of these alters the speed. Andante tranquillo is andante, played calmly.
teach.didYouKnow: Semplice is the rarest instruction of the group, and the hardest to follow. It asks a player to stop interpreting, which takes more discipline than any amount of expression.

lessons.title: Extremes, and marks on the page

objectives: Recognise the Grade 3 tempo extremes and the marks that direct a repeat
-issimo pushes a word to its extreme
Prima and seconda volta are the first-time and second-time bars

concept.title: The far ends, and where to look
concept.body: Two of these push a tempo word to its limit: *adagissimo* is very slow and *prestissimo* as fast as possible, the *-issimo* ending doing the same job it does in fortissimo. *Allargando* broadens, and *tempo rubato* gives the player freedom with the time — literally 'stolen time', taken from one note and paid back to another. *Ad libitum* leaves a passage to the player's choice. *Subito* means suddenly, so subito piano is an instant drop, and *sotto voce* asks for an undertone. The rest are marks on the page rather than instructions in words: *marcato* emphasises a note, and *prima volta* and *seconda volta* are the first-time and second-time bars that tell you which ending to take on a repeat.

teach.smartTip: -issimo means 'most'. It works the same on prestissimo as it does on fortissimo.
teach.didYouKnow: Rubato means stolen. The old rule was that time borrowed from one note had to be repaid to another, so the bar still lasted exactly as long — the freedom was inside the bar, not on top of it.

lessons.title: Harmonic minor in the new keys

objectives: Harmonic minor is still the natural (key-signature) minor with the 7th note raised a semitone — now in six more keys
Two of the new raised 7ths spell unusual accidentals: F♯ minor's is E♯ (not F), and C♯ minor's is B♯ (not C)
C minor's raised 7th is B♮ and F minor's is E♮ — raising a flatted degree can land back on a natural

concept.title: Harmonic minor in the new keys
concept.body: The same rule as before — raise the natural minor's 7th note a semitone — now applies to six more keys. Most of the new raised 7ths look as you'd expect: B minor's is A♯, G minor's is F♯. But the two sharp-tonic keys spell their raised 7th on the 7th letter even when that means an enharmonic-of-natural spelling: F♯ minor's raised 7th is E♯ (not F), and C♯ minor's is B♯ (not C). Meanwhile C minor's raised 7th is B♮ and F minor's is E♮ — raising a flatted note can land you back on a natural.

teach.smartTip: Always spell the raised 7th on the 7th letter of the scale, never on a different letter — that's why F♯ minor's raised 7th is written E♯, not F natural.
teach.didYouKnow: E♯ and B♯ look unusual on the stave, but they're the correct, exam-expected spellings — writing F natural or C natural instead would name the wrong letter of the scale entirely.

objectives: Melodic minor is directional: it raises the 6th and 7th notes going up, but reverts to natural minor coming down
The ascending and descending forms genuinely differ — the note you play going up is not always the note you play coming down
Melodic minor applies to every minor key you know so far, not just the six new ones

concept.title: The melodic minor scale
concept.body: Melodic minor is the only minor form that changes with direction. Going up, it raises the 6th and 7th notes a semitone above the key signature, smoothing over the augmented 2nd that harmonic minor leaves between them. Coming down, both revert to natural minor — the plain key-signature 6th and 7th. So E melodic minor ascends E F♯ G A B C♯ D♯ E, but descends E D♮ C♮ B A G F♯ E: the raised C♯ and D♯ of the ascent return to C♮ and D♮ on the way down. This directional form applies to every minor key in this course, including A, E and D minor from Grade 2.

teach.smartTip: Check the direction before you check the notes — a melodic minor scale's ascending and descending forms are genuinely different, not a memory slip.
teach.didYouKnow: Melodic minor's ascending form was designed to smooth out the awkward augmented-2nd leap of harmonic minor, which makes melodies harder to sing — the descending form then simply reverts to natural minor, since that leap isn't a problem going down.

objectives: How to tell a simple time signature from a compound one
Why 6/8 has six quavers but only two beats
The dotted crotchet as the compound beat

concept.title: Simple time and compound time
concept.body: Every time signature belongs to one of two families, and the top number tells you which. A top number of 2, 3 or 4 is simple time: each beat splits into two equal halves, so 3/4 is three crotchet beats and each one divides into two quavers. A top number of 6, 9 or 12 is compound time: each beat splits into three, and the beat itself is a dotted note. So 6/8 is not six beats — it is six quavers grouped into two dotted-crotchet beats, counted 1 2 3 · 4 5 6. In the same way 9/8 has three dotted-crotchet beats and 12/8 has four.

teach.smartTip: Feel 6/8 as a gentle two, not a fast six — like the swing of "merri-ly, merri-ly".
teach.didYouKnow: Many famous lullabies and jigs are in 6/8 — its lilting two-in-a-bar sway is why it feels like rocking.

theoryInSound.prompt: Play the bar and tap on each strong beat you hear.

objectives: How 9/8 and 12/8 extend the dotted-crotchet beat to three and four beats a bar
Counting the dotted-crotchet beats in a hidden-signature bar to work out which compound metre it's in
The demisemiquaver — half a semiquaver — as the next step down the compound note tree

concept.title: Counting 9/8 and 12/8
concept.body: 9/8 and 12/8 work the same way as 6/8 — the beat is still a dotted crotchet, made of three quavers. 9/8 groups its nine quavers into three dotted-crotchet beats; 12/8 groups its twelve quavers into four. To find which one you're looking at, add up the dotted-crotchet beats in the bar rather than counting quavers one by one. The note tree keeps dividing too: a demisemiquaver is half a semiquaver, the smallest value you'll meet at this grade.

teach.smartTip: Count the dotted-crotchet beats, not the quavers — three beats means 9/8, four means 12/8.
teach.didYouKnow: Demisemiquavers are rare outside fast, decorative passages — composers reach for them to write a flourish, not a steady pulse.

objectives: The quaver, semiquaver and demisemiquaver rests match the quaver, semiquaver and demisemiquaver notes
Each smaller rest is written with one more hook than the one above it, just as each smaller note gains a tail
Fill a gap by matching its exact length — a shorter silence needs a shorter rest

concept.title: The shorter rests
concept.body: The smaller note values each have a matching rest. A quaver rest lasts half a beat, a semiquaver rest a quarter, a demisemiquaver rest an eighth. Their symbols echo the notes: as the note gains a tail, the rest gains a hook — one for the quaver rest, two for the semiquaver, three for the demisemiquaver. To complete a bar, find how much time is missing and pick the rest of exactly that length.

teach.smartTip: Count the hooks: one hook is a quaver rest, two a semiquaver, three a demisemiquaver — the same order as the notes' tails.
teach.didYouKnow: The demisemiquaver rest packs three hooks onto a tiny symbol — beyond it lie the hemidemisemiquaver rest and its four hooks, rarely seen outside virtuoso flourishes.

objectives: Compound time beams its quavers in threes, one group per dotted beat
6/8 and 3/4 hold the same six quavers and differ only in the beams
The number of beams equals the number of beats

concept.title: Threes, not twos
concept.body: A compound beat is a dotted crotchet, which divides into three quavers rather than two. So 6/8 beams its six quavers as two groups of three, 9/8 as three groups, and 12/8 as four. This is the clearest difference between 6/8 and 3/4 on the page: both bars hold six quavers and last the same time, but 3/4 beams them in twos for three crotchet beats and 6/8 in threes for two dotted beats. Nothing else in the notation distinguishes them, so the beams carry the whole meaning. Count the groups and you have counted the beats.

teach.smartTip: Count the beamed groups, not the quavers. Each group is one dotted beat.
teach.didYouKnow: The 6/8 and 3/4 pairing is the whole joke of "America" in West Side Story, which alternates the two on identical notes.

objectives: Every interval above the tonic has both a number (2nd, 3rd... octave) and a quality — perfect, major, or minor
4ths, 5ths and octaves are always perfect; 2nds, 3rds, 6ths and 7ths take a major or minor label
A minor key's 3rd, 6th and 7th above the tonic are a semitone smaller than a major key's — that's what makes them minor

concept.title: Naming interval quality
concept.body: Every interval above the tonic has a number and a quality. 4ths, 5ths and octaves are always perfect — there's no major or minor version of them. 2nds, 3rds, 6ths and 7ths take a major or minor label. Above a major-key tonic they are all major; above a minor-key tonic the 3rd, 6th and 7th shrink by a semitone to minor, while the 2nd stays major. Compare a 3rd in both key types and you'll hear the difference: a major 3rd sounds bright, a minor 3rd sounds darker.

teach.smartTip: Check the key signature first — above a major tonic every 2nd, 3rd, 6th and 7th is major; above a minor tonic, they're minor instead.
teach.didYouKnow: Perfect intervals (unison, 4th, 5th, octave) get their name because their simple, pure ratios sounded "perfect" to early theorists — they never take a major or minor label.

lessons.title: Ledger lines — notes beyond the stave

objectives: How ledger lines extend the stave one line at a time, above and below
Counting outward in 3rds — line, space, line — from a landmark note you already know
The newly reachable notes: F3 up to E6 in the treble clef, A1 up to G4 in the bass clef

concept.title: Reading ledger-line notes
concept.body: Ledger lines are short extra lines that continue the stave, one at a time, above or below it. Rather than counting every ledger line from scratch, count outward in 3rds — line, space, line — from a landmark you already know: middle C sits on its own ledger line, just below the treble stave and just above the bass stave. Working outward this way now reaches one ledger line further than Grade 2 — down to F3 and up to E6 in the treble clef, and down to A1 and up to G4 in the bass clef.

teach.smartTip: Count in 3rds from a landmark you already know, not ledger line by ledger line from the stave — line to space to line gets you there in half the steps.
teach.didYouKnow: Ledger lines have no upper limit — orchestral parts for piccolo or double bass sometimes stack five or six of them, though this course never asks for more than one beyond Grade 2's range.

objectives: Read a passage that uses the wider Grade 3 range
Identify the metre when it may be compound
Answer several different questions about one passage

concept.title: One passage, several questions
concept.body: The passage grows with the grade. At Grade 3 it can reach further above and below the stave, and it can be in compound time, so the metre question is no longer a choice between three simple signatures. The method does not change. Read the clef, then the key signature, then the time signature, and work out whether the beat divides in two or in three before you count anything. A question about the highest note is a reading question; a question about the longest note is a note-value question; a question about the metre is a counting question. Recognising which kind of question you have been asked is most of the work.

teach.smartTip: Clef, key signature, time signature, then notes. The same order every time.
teach.didYouKnow: Examiners write the general-observation question last, after the rest of the paper is set, so that it uses only what the paper has already asked about.

objectives: What an anacrusis (upbeat) is — one or more notes that lead into the first full bar
Why the first partial bar and the final bar together always make one complete bar
How to count the beats in the upbeat from the stave

concept.title: Starting before the first full bar
concept.body: An anacrusis — an upbeat — is a run-up of notes before the first full bar, landing on the first strong beat. Because that opening bar is short, it has "borrowed" beats from a full bar's worth; the piece pays them back with a matching short bar at the very end, so the first bar and the last bar together always add up to exactly one whole bar. To find how many beats are in the upbeat, count the beats from the start of the piece to the first barline.

teach.smartTip: Count backwards from the first barline to the very first note — however many beats that takes is the length of the upbeat.
teach.didYouKnow: Plenty of familiar songs start on an upbeat — "Hap-py birth-day to you" begins on the third beat of the bar — which is why the word anacrusis comes from the Greek for "striking up".

lessons.title: Octave transposition — treble to bass and back

objectives: What octave transposition means — the same melody, rewritten a perfect octave away, in the opposite clef
Why every letter name stays exactly the same — only the octave number moves, never the letter
The fixed direction for each clef pair: treble down an octave into the bass clef, bass up an octave into the treble clef

concept.title: Rewriting a melody an octave away
concept.body: Octave transposition means rewriting a melody a perfect octave away, in the opposite clef, while keeping every letter name and rhythm exactly the same. A melody given in the treble clef is rewritten one octave **lower** in the bass clef; a melody given in the bass clef is rewritten one octave **higher** in the treble clef. Every note keeps its letter name — only its octave number changes, so a treble G4 becomes a bass G3, never a different letter. Copy the rhythm note for note too: same durations, same dots, same barlines — only the pitches move.

teach.smartTip: Keep the letter name and just move it one octave — a G stays a G, never becomes an A or an F, even though it lands on a different line or space on the new stave.
teach.didYouKnow: Octave transposition is the simplest kind of transposition, because the letter names never change — later grades add transposing to a different key altogether, like a clarinet in B♭ reading its part a tone higher than it actually sounds.
